title: Subject-verb agreement with a hidden subject
subtitle: Form, Structure, and Sense · 51 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **51 of the official questions in Form, Structure, and Sense are this one** — 19 Easy, 16 Medium, 16 Hard.
Most versions sit at the Easy tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- The blank sits right where the main verb goes, and all four choices are the same verb in different number and tense forms, such as singular and plural 'is/are/was/were/has/have'.

- Between the true subject and the blank there is usually a long prepositional phrase, an appositive between commas or dashes, or a relative clause, and that clutter ends in a noun whose number differs from the subject's.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Cross out every prepositional phrase ('of...', 'with...', 'from...to...'), anything between commas or dashes, and any 'which/who' clause.
- 2) Name the one noun that actually does the verb, and decide whether it is singular or plural.
- Treat 'every', 'each', 'one of', or a possessive like 'X's use' as singular.
- 3) Choose the choice that matches that number.
- If two choices still match, choose the plain tense that fits the rest of the sentence.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: The wrong choices agree with whatever noun sits right before the blank, such as the plural object of 'of' or a plural list inside an appositive.
They also play on subjects that feel plural but are grammatically singular: a named organization, 'every last X', 'one of several', or a possessive noun phrase whose head is singular.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
The wrong choices agree with whatever noun sits right before the blank, such as the plural object of 'of' or a plural list inside an appositive.
They also play on subjects that feel plural but are grammatically singular: a named organization, 'every last X', 'one of several', or a possessive noun phrase whose head is singular.
